Y5.value:
Eugène Grasset was a leading figure in the French Art Nouveau poster movement, admired for his dazzling, multi-colored lithographs that combined striking palettes with a sharp, dramatic presence. This 1894 work features Sarah Bernhardt, the most celebrated actress of her era, whose magnetic stage presence and daring choices — from playing tragic heroines like Phèdre and Marguerite Gautier to taking on Hamlet in French — made her a legend. Beyond the stage, she toured internationally, ran her own Paris theater, and even continued performing after the amputation of her leg, cementing her reputation as an unstoppable force of art and willpower.

Although Bernhardt never actually played Joan of Arc, the decision to depict her as the saintly heroine was a deliberate act of myth-making. By aligning her with Joan — a national symbol of courage and purity — Grasset’s lithograph reinforced her image as larger than life. Bernhardt moved in the highest artistic circles, admired by Victor Hugo, painted by Gustave Doré, and befriended by writers and painters who saw her as a muse. The combination of her legendary persona and Grasset’s innovative artistry makes this piece not only visually captivating, but also a fascinating snapshot of fin-de-siècle France — a true standout in any collection of Art Nouveau poster art.

Y6.value:
"Exodus into Space (plate 4)" (1971–72) is a screenprint by the Austrian artist Friedensreich Hundertwasser, a visionary painter, architect, and environmental activist. The work reflects Hundertwasser’s fascination with humanity’s place in the cosmos, created during the height of the Space Race, when artists worldwide were responding to humankind’s exploration beyond Earth. True to his style, it combines vibrant colors, organic forms, and metallic embossing—elements that emphasize his rejection of straight lines and industrial rigidity. Produced in a limited edition of 300, this piece highlights Hundertwasser’s commitment to merging art with philosophy, ecology, and utopian ideas of a harmonious future. 

Hundertwasser prints regularly draw attention due to their multitude of colors and imaginitve design elements. A self declared naturist Hundertwasser (Austrian) believed art and design should follow the truth of the natural world and shouldn't feature human ideals in the forms of right angles or straight lines. In essence his art is a call to meld with the natural world and in turn evokes a certain psychadelic feel. A pioneer of these types of visionary styles he is vastly over looked outside of Europe where he designed countless buildings and public works and is a household name. His prints are among the most extravigent to exist in the fine art market, many featuring more than 20 layers of printing and  they consistently elicit the curiosity of any art enthusiast. The Regntag (Rainy Day) is perhaps his most famous suite of works, 10 in total, bearing the namesake of his sea vessel. There is a short art film produced by the artist that bears the name as well.

Y7.value: Robert Indiana’s “New York State Theatre / Lincoln Center” poster (1964) was created to celebrate the dedication of the New York State Theater at Lincoln Center on April 23, 1964, designed by architect Philip Johnson. Indiana, best known for his bold typographic “LOVE” works, brought his Pop Art sensibility to cultural institutions at a moment when New York was cementing its role as a global center for both modern art and performance. This poster was published in an edition of about 500, alongside a smaller limited edition of 144, making it relatively accessible compared to his fine art prints. It stands as a vivid example of how Indiana merged graphic design with high art, elevating posters to collectible objects that bridged art, theater, and public life in 1960s New York.

Y8.value: Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s Wrapped Monument to Vittorio Emanuele belongs to their broader practice of “wrapping” monuments, buildings, and landscapes to provoke new ways of seeing familiar forms. Created in 1975 as an exhibition poster for Galeria Ciento in Barcelona, it reflects their early European projects before their monumental wrappings in Paris and Berlin. The act of covering a statue of Vittorio Emanuele II—Italy’s first king—invited reflection on national memory, power, and the shifting meaning of public monuments. Today, such works are considered precursors to later large-scale interventions, like the wrapping of the Pont Neuf in Paris (1985) and the Reichstag in Berlin (1995).

Y9.value: Peter Blake, often called the “Godfather of Pop Art,” is best known for co-creating the iconic album cover for The Beatles’ Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band in 1967. By the late 1990s, when Demonstrations in a Department Store I was created, Blake was revisiting themes of consumerism and mass culture that had defined his earlier Pop Art career. This screenprint reflects his interest in everyday objects and commercial spaces, echoing his fascination with how consumer goods shape modern identity. Published by Gresham Studio in Cambridge, UK, the edition highlights Blake’s enduring role in bridging fine art and popular culture into the 21st century.

Y10.value: Jim Dine’s Jerusalem Plant #4 (1982) is part of his broader exploration of plants and botanical imagery, a theme that often carried symbolic weight in his work. Dine was a central figure in the Pop Art movement, but unlike many of his contemporaries, he infused personal and emotional meaning into his imagery, frequently revisiting motifs such as hearts, tools, and plants. This print was created at Universal Limited Art Editions (ULAE), a prestigious American print workshop that collaborated with leading modern artists like Jasper Johns and Robert Rauschenberg. The use of hand-painting on top of lithography reflects Dine’s interest in blending unique painterly gestures with reproducible printmaking, giving each impression a distinct quality.

Y11.value: Friedensreich Hundertwasser was an Austrian artist and architect known for his vibrant, organic forms and rejection of straight lines, which he called “the devil’s tools.” This 1972 screenprint, Hommage à Schröder-Sonnenstern, pays tribute to the eccentric German outsider artist Friedrich Schröder-Sonnenstern, celebrated for his fantastical and surreal imagery. Produced by the respected Dietz Offizin workshop and published by Ars Viva in Zurich, the work exemplifies Hundertwasser’s experiments with unconventional materials, incorporating metal imprints and electrostatic felt fibrils. His prints from this period reflect his philosophy of merging art, nature, and individuality, breaking away from rigid modernist traditions.

Y12.value: Three Bathers (1922–1923) is a lithograph by George Wesley Bellows, an American artist associated with the Ashcan School, known for capturing raw and energetic scenes of early 20th-century life. Bellows frequently explored the human figure, and his bathers series reflected his fascination with the body in motion, often set in natural landscapes. Lithography was a medium he particularly enjoyed, as it allowed for expressive lines and tonal contrasts that suited his vigorous style. This work came near the end of his career—Bellows died unexpectedly in 1925 at only 42, making pieces from this period especially significant in his oeuvre.

Y13.value: Emil Ganso (1895–1941) was a German-born American artist known for his masterful etchings, drypoints, and woodcuts, often focusing on intimate nudes and still lifes. He immigrated to the U.S. in 1912, working as a baker before fully dedicating himself to art. By the 1930s, Ganso had gained national recognition, with his work included in exhibitions at institutions like the Whitney Museum and the Art Institute of Chicago. His prints, such as Hilda (1930), demonstrate his skill in combining delicacy of line with bold tonal contrasts, hallmarks of the American printmaking renaissance during that era.

Y14.value: Emil Ganso (1895–1941) was a German-born American artist known for his mastery of printmaking, particularly etchings, aquatints, and woodcuts. His work often captured scenes of everyday life with a modernist sensibility, and he became associated with the American Artists’ Group (AAG), which helped make fine art more accessible to the public during the 1930s and 1940s. The etching Sunbath (1936) reflects the era’s interest in leisure and the human figure, while also showcasing the rich tonal effects achievable with aquatint. Ganso’s works were widely collected in his lifetime, and he contributed to the democratization of art through affordable editions like this one.

Y15.value: Lester Hornby (1882–1956) was an American artist and printmaker known for his mastery of etching and drypoint, often incorporating color into his works at a time when black-and-white etching was the norm. His subject Cheri (1906) reflects Hornby’s time in Paris, where he studied and worked among the city’s vibrant artistic community in Montparnasse. The limited edition of just 30 impressions, each signed and estate stamped, shows how early 20th-century printmakers sought to elevate etchings into collectible fine art rather than mass reproductions. Hornby’s works are now regarded as important examples of the transatlantic exchange of artistic ideas between France and America in the early modernist era.

Y16.value: James McBey (1883–1959) was a Scottish artist celebrated for his etchings and drypoints, often compared to Whistler. His 1939 etching Manhattan captures the iconic New York skyline on the eve of World War II, at a time when skyscrapers symbolized modernity and American progress. McBey created a very limited number of proofs—this piece belongs to the rare first published state of only 73 impressions, produced before the artist altered the sky by burnishing out the clouds. Collectors value works like this not only for their technical mastery but also as snapshots of a rapidly changing era in both art and world history.

Y18.value: John J. A. Murphy was an American artist and printmaker known for his woodblock prints during the early 20th century, often blending modernist design with traditional printmaking techniques. His work, such as Faces and Figures from the 1920s–30s, reflects the influence of the Arts and Crafts movement, which emphasized handcrafted quality and fine detail. Woodblock self-portraits like this one also highlight the growing interest in self-representation among modern artists, who were exploring their identity through their craft. At the time, Murphy’s prints were exhibited alongside other American modernists and helped bring renewed attention to the woodcut medium in the United States.

Y19.value: Louis Schanker was a prominent American abstract artist and a founding member of the New York art group known as The Ten, who in the 1930s challenged conservative art institutions by promoting modernist approaches. His lithographs, including Café (1938), were produced during the Works Progress Administration (WPA) era, when artists were commissioned to create affordable art for the public. Schanker’s work combined elements of Cubism and abstraction, often using bold colors and geometric forms to convey rhythm and movement. Limited editions like this signed and numbered print reflect both the democratization of art during the Depression and the artist’s role in shaping early American modernism.

Y20.value: William Strasser was a mid-20th century American artist known for his printmaking, particularly monoprints and lithographs. A monoprint like On the River is a unique print made by painting or inking directly onto a plate, so each impression is one-of-a-kind—quite different from standard edition prints. During the postwar period, many artists in the U.S. embraced experimental printmaking as a way to blend painterly expression with reproducible art, and Strasser’s works often reflect this modernist exploration. Collectors value pieces like this both for their scarcity and for the way they embody the creative experimentation of American printmakers in the 1950s–60s.

Y21.value: Verve was a groundbreaking French art magazine founded in 1937 by publisher Tériade, who worked closely with many of the greatest modern artists of the 20th century. The publication was celebrated for its luxurious lithographic plates, often created directly by artists such as Henri Matisse, Marc Chagall, and Georges Braque, making each issue itself a work of art. Along with Derrière Le Miroir, another important artist-focused periodical, Verve provided an accessible yet high-quality platform for avant-garde art at a time when Europe was undergoing immense cultural and political upheaval. Collections of prints from these magazines remain highly sought after because they encapsulate the vibrancy of modernism and preserve original works by some of the most influential artists of the century.

Y22.value: Martial Raysse (b. 1936) is a French artist closely associated with the Nouveau Réalisme movement, often considered the European counterpart to American Pop Art. His works frequently draw on themes of consumerism, mythology, and classical imagery reinterpreted through vibrant modern aesthetics. Enlèvement d’Europe (The Abduction of Europa) revisits the ancient myth of Europa and Zeus, a subject that has inspired artists since antiquity, but Raysse reimagines it through the lens of 20th-century visual culture. By the late 1980s, when this print was created, Raysse was already internationally recognized for blending mythological subjects with bold colors and playful irony, making this lithograph a striking example of his mature style.

Y23.value: John James Audubon (1785–1851) is one of the most celebrated naturalists and wildlife illustrators of the 19th century, best known for his monumental Birds of America. After completing that project, he turned his attention to mammals, collaborating with his sons to create The Viviparous Quadrupeds of North America (1845–1854). The Lepus Americanus (Northern Hare) plate was produced by J.T. Bowen in Philadelphia, using hand-colored lithography to capture both scientific accuracy and aesthetic beauty. These prints were among the earliest comprehensive attempts to document North American mammals, making them prized by collectors not only for their artistry but also for their importance in the history of natural science.

E24.value: The American Federation of Art 80th Anniversary 1909-1989

Y24.value: Roy Lichtenstein, one of the leading figures of the Pop Art movement, was known for his comic-inspired works that challenged the divide between high and low art. This poster was created in 1989 to celebrate the 80th anniversary of the American Federation of Arts, an organization founded in 1909 to make art more accessible to the public. Lichtenstein often revisited and reinterpreted earlier works, which is why this piece is marked “After,” signifying it was based on an existing design rather than an entirely original composition. Posters like this not only highlight his bold style but also reflect the broader cultural effort to democratize art appreciation during the late 20th century.

Y25.value: La Sibylle de Cumes (1928) after Georges Rouault reflects the artist’s deep engagement with spiritual and mystical themes, which were central to his practice. Rouault, originally trained as a stained-glass artist, carried the influence of bold outlines and luminous colors into his paintings and prints, giving them a distinctive, almost medieval quality. The subject—the Cumaean Sibyl—was a prophetic figure from classical antiquity, later woven into Christian iconography through her association with foretelling the coming of Christ. Works like this highlight Rouault’s ability to bridge ancient myth, religious symbolism, and modern expressionist style, making his art resonate with both historical depth and emotional immediacy.

Y26.value: Zao Wou-Ki was a Chinese-French painter celebrated for blending traditional Chinese ink painting techniques with European abstract expressionism. By the 1980s, when The Orchid plate was created, he was internationally recognized and had begun exploring ceramics as an extension of his artistic language. The orchid motif carries deep symbolism in Chinese culture, often associated with elegance, refinement, and scholarly virtue. This earthenware plate reflects both his cross-cultural identity and his ability to translate lyrical abstraction into decorative arts beyond canvas.

Y27.value: Oskar Kokoschka’s Apulia (1964) is a portfolio of twenty lithographs inspired by his travels through the Apulia region of southern Italy, an area rich with ancient ruins, Romanesque churches, and Mediterranean landscapes. Kokoschka, a leading figure of Austrian Expressionism, often captured the vitality and psychological intensity of places and people, and here he translated the region’s history and atmosphere into expressive, gestural prints. Published by Marlborough Fine Art in London, the edition was limited to just 50 sets, each signed and numbered by the artist, underscoring its rarity. This body of work also reflects Kokoschka’s postwar career, during which he devoted significant attention to printmaking as a means of combining his painterly style with broader dissemination of his art.

Y28.value: Maurice de Vlaminck was a French painter closely associated with Fauvism, a movement known for its vivid colors and expressive brushwork. By the 1950s, when Village sous la neige (Saint-Maurice-lès-Charence) was produced, he had moved toward a more restrained palette, often depicting rural French landscapes with a somber, atmospheric mood. The heliogravure technique allowed for richly textured reproductions that captured the painterly qualities of his original works. This piece reflects Vlaminck’s later career, when he turned to quieter, wintry village scenes that conveyed both nostalgia and a deep connection to the French countryside.

Y29.value: The Tufted Duck print you’re looking at is based on the work of John James Audubon, the famed naturalist and painter best known for his monumental series The Birds of America (1827–1838). Audubon’s plates were originally produced as hand-colored aquatints, a labor-intensive process involving skilled engravers and colorists, making each print both a scientific record and a work of art. While the Tufted Duck itself is a Eurasian species and relatively rare in North America, Audubon sought to include it to give his series a comprehensive scope. Today, surviving original plates and even high-quality later impressions remain highly valued by collectors, blending ornithological history with fine art.

Y30.value: Marc Chagall was a Russian-French modernist whose work often blended elements of Cubism, Fauvism, and Surrealism, creating dreamlike compositions infused with folklore and personal symbolism. He experimented widely with printmaking techniques, and his etchings in particular are prized for their expressive linework and lyrical, often mystical imagery. Chagall began working seriously with etching in the 1920s, producing illustrations for literary classics such as La Fontaine’s Fables and the Bible. Even a smaller, unsigned or uncertainly signed etching reflects his distinctive hand and remains sought after for its connection to one of the most imaginative artists of the 20th century.

Y31.value: Léonard Tsuguharu Foujita was a Japanese–French painter and printmaker who became a celebrated figure in Paris during the 1920s, blending Japanese ink techniques with Western modernist styles. His Book of Cats (1929), from which Chanton Assis originates, is considered one of the most beautiful and desirable illustrated books of the 20th century, featuring 20 collotypes of cats rendered with exquisite delicacy. Foujita’s cats were deeply personal—he often lived surrounded by them—and he captured their elegance and mischievous spirit with an unmatched sensitivity. The edition quickly sold out on publication, and today, individual plates are highly collectible, valued both for their rarity and their role in cementing Foujita’s reputation as the great “painter of cats.”

E32.value: Oh what a Taylor can do

Y32.value: Francisco de Goya’s etching Oh What a Tailor Can Do (Qué tal sastre!) comes from his famous satirical series Los Caprichos (1799), a set of 80 prints critiquing social folly, superstition, and corruption in late 18th-century Spain. This particular plate mocks vanity and the absurdities of fashion, portraying human weakness with biting humor. Goya used aquatint and etching to achieve striking contrasts of light and shadow, a technical mastery that gave his social commentary a haunting intensity. Though the series was withdrawn shortly after publication due to fear of Inquisition backlash, it went on to become one of the most influential works in Western printmaking.

Y33.value: Fairfield Porter was an American painter and printmaker best known for his lyrical, representational style at a time when Abstract Expressionism dominated the art world. He often depicted domestic interiors, portraits of friends, and serene landscapes, balancing a modernist sensibility with an appreciation for everyday beauty. Apple Blossom III (1974) reflects his love of nature and his subtle use of color to create harmony and intimacy within a scene. Produced as a limited-edition lithograph late in his career, works like this highlight Porter’s enduring commitment to figuration and his influence on a generation of realist painters who followed.

Y34.value: Fairfield Porter’s Isle au Haut (1975) captures the quiet, contemplative landscapes of coastal Maine, where he spent many summers painting. Porter had a deep connection to Maine’s islands, and Isle au Haut—a remote and rugged spot—reflects his sensitivity to light, color, and natural atmosphere. This lithograph was published by Brooke Alexander, Inc., a key figure in promoting contemporary printmaking in New York during the 1970s, and printed by the renowned American Atelier. As one of Porter’s later prints, it demonstrates his ability to translate his painterly vision into lithography, preserving the freshness and intimacy that define his best work.

Y35.value: Otto Dix’s Internationaler Reitakt (1922) is a powerful drypoint from the years immediately following World War I, when the artist was producing some of his most biting and socially critical works. Dix, a veteran himself, became a leading figure of the Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity) movement, using unflinching realism to expose the brutality, decadence, and absurdity of postwar German society. His prints from this period often combine sharp satire with raw psychological intensity, and the drypoint technique—with its rich burr and dark plate tone—amplifies that visceral effect. Limited to just 50 impressions, this work exemplifies Dix’s fearless engagement with the cultural upheaval of Weimar Germany.

Y36.value: Otto Dix’s Technisches Personal (1922) comes from the same fertile postwar period as Internationaler Reitakt, when he turned to printmaking to deliver some of his most searing critiques of modern life. The title, meaning “technical staff,” reflects Dix’s fascination with the mechanization and depersonalization of society in the aftermath of World War I. Using the drypoint medium, he achieved intense textures and dramatic contrasts, with the burr of the line giving the image a raw, almost abrasive energy. As with many of his works from the early 1920s, the print exemplifies Dix’s role as a chronicler of Weimar Germany’s unsettling blend of technological progress, social change, and lingering trauma.

Y37.value: Emil Nolde’s Frau N. (Frau Ada Nolde) (1911) is an intimate etching and drypoint portrait of his wife, Ada, who was a frequent subject and an important muse throughout his career. Nolde, a leading figure of German Expressionism and a member of Die Brücke, brought an emotional intensity to his printmaking, using rough, expressive lines and dramatic contrasts to convey psychological depth. The combination of etching and drypoint gave his portraits a raw immediacy, with the plate tone adding to their atmospheric quality. With only about 20 impressions known, this rare print reflects both Nolde’s devotion to Ada and his innovative role in elevating printmaking as a modern expressive art form.

Y38.value: Man Ray’s L’Aventure (1972) reflects the artist’s lifelong engagement with experimentation, symbolism, and the playful crossing of boundaries between art and life. Best known as a central figure in Dada and Surrealism, Man Ray brought his inventive spirit to printmaking later in his career, using etching and aquatint to explore bold color and form. Produced in Paris and published in Brussels, the print exemplifies his international presence and enduring influence on avant-garde art well into the 20th century. With its limited edition of just 90 impressions, L’Aventure captures the wit, imagination, and unconventional approach that made Man Ray one of the most original figures of modernism.

Y39.value: Lill Tschudi’s Nudes (1933) is a striking example of her mastery of the linocut, a medium she helped elevate within modern printmaking. A Swiss artist associated with the Grosvenor School of Modern Art in London, Tschudi was part of the pioneering group that used linocut to create bold, dynamic compositions in vivid colors. While she is often celebrated for her depictions of urban life and movement, Nudes shows her ability to apply the same rhythmic energy and stylized forms to the human figure. Printed in a sophisticated palette on delicate oriental paper, this rare edition of just 50 impressions demonstrates both her technical finesse and her central role in the modernist printmaking revival of the 1930s.

Y40.value: Marc Chagall’s Le profil et l’enfant rouge (1960) is a luminous lithograph created during one of the most prolific periods of his career, when he collaborated extensively with the master printer Fernand Mourlot in Paris. This work was included in Chagall Lithographe, Tome I, a landmark volume that helped establish his reputation as one of the greatest modern printmakers. Chagall’s lithographs are celebrated for their dreamlike quality, rich colors, and fusion of personal memory, folklore, and biblical symbolism—often evoking a sense of poetic wonder. With its small edition size and connection to the deluxe publication, this piece exemplifies the technical brilliance and imaginative spirit that made Chagall’s graphic works so influential in 20th-century art.

Y41.value: Takeshi Murakami’s Hypha (2007) reflects his signature blending of contemporary pop culture with traditional Japanese artistic sensibilities, a style often described as “Superflat.” The title references the branching filaments of fungi, which grow and spread invisibly—an idea Murakami has linked to how art and ideas permeate global culture. By the mid-2000s, Murakami was already an international art star, collaborating with major brands like Louis Vuitton and shaping the intersection of fine art and commercial design. Works like Hypha embody both playful surface appeal and deeper commentary on organic growth, globalization, and the interconnectedness of cultural production.

Y42.value: Takashi Murakami’s A Picture of the Blessed Lion Who Stares at Death (2009) is a striking example of his fusion of Buddhist iconography with contemporary pop aesthetics. The lion, a traditional guardian figure in East Asian art and temples, is reimagined through Murakami’s vivid colors and stylized forms, embodying both strength and spiritual transcendence. Created under his Kaikai Kiki studio in Tokyo, the work reflects his practice of producing limited-edition prints that make his art accessible while maintaining high artistic value. This piece also illustrates Murakami’s ongoing dialogue between life, death, and enlightenment, central themes in his body of work that bridge tradition and modernity.

Y43.value: Takashi Murakami’s And then, when that’s done… (2009) continues his exploration of the iconic “DOB” character, often interpreted as an alter ego and commentary on the commercialization of contemporary culture. Rendered here as an offset lithograph, the work exemplifies Murakami’s “Superflat” aesthetic, merging the slick surfaces of pop art with the layered references of traditional Japanese painting. The character’s wide-eyed, almost manic expression embodies both playful charm and unsettling intensity, reflecting Murakami’s interest in the dualities of innocence and anxiety within modern society. Published by Kaikai Kiki Co., Ltd. in Tokyo and produced in a limited edition of 300, the print underscores Murakami’s commitment to making his art accessible to a broad audience while retaining the exclusivity of fine art production. Exhibited and sold internationally, this piece demonstrates the enduring appeal of Murakami’s visual language, which seamlessly bridges high art, mass media, and global consumer culture.

Y48.value: Franz Marc’s Schlafende Hirtin (1912) is a rare woodcut from the artist’s groundbreaking Der Blaue Reiter period. With its simplified forms and lyrical symbolism, the print reflects Marc’s search for spiritual harmony between humanity and nature. This impression, authenticated by Maria Marc’s signature and the estate stamp, is characteristic of the very limited editions that survive. A cornerstone of German Expressionist printmaking, it offers collectors a scarce opportunity to acquire a work that embodies both Marc’s artistic vision and the enduring legacy of early modernism.

Y49.value: Sir William Russell Flint’s Slippery Steps exemplifies the artist’s mastery of the etched line and his enduring fascination with atmosphere, elegance, and movement. Executed with exquisite control, the composition captures a fleeting, light-struck moment typical of Flint’s celebrated portrayals of women in intimate European settings. Printed on fine Whatman paper and delicately hand-signed by the artist, this impression conveys the silken tonal transitions and crisp draughtsmanship that define Flint’s best graphic work. Issued in a small numbered edition, Slippery Steps represents Flint’s ability to merge technical precision with poetic grace. For collectors of early-twentieth-century British etching, it stands as both a testament to the artist’s refinement and a touchstone of the “etching revival” that placed Flint among the leading printmakers of his generation.

Y50.value: Screenprint on paper, pencil-signed lower right, artist’s proof 4/15. Created in 1997, Nathaniel Bustion’s African Girl embodies the artist’s vibrant engagement with identity, rhythm, and cultural memory. Using the layered luminosity of the screenprint medium, Bustion distills his subject into bold planes of color and sculptural contour, evoking both modernist abstraction and the visual cadences of African art. The poised figure—at once iconic and intimate—reflects Bustion’s lifelong exploration of Black womanhood and the strength and dignity of everyday experience. Printed in a rare artist’s proof edition of only fifteen impressions, this work demonstrates the meticulous craft and expressive power that define Bustion’s late-twentieth-century practice. With its dynamic balance of form and hue, African Girl stands as a compelling testament to the artist’s vision—bridging modern printmaking technique and the affirming spirit of the African diaspora in contemporary American art.

Y52.value: Käthe Kollwitz’s Selbstbildnis (1912) is one of the artist’s most intimate and widely recognized etched self-portraits, executed at the height of her mature period. Printed in sepia aquatint and etching, this striking image belongs to the scarce Emil Richter edition of thirty impressions issued circa 1920. Each was hand-signed by Kollwitz, reflecting her personal oversight of the printing. The work demonstrates her masterful balance of strength and vulnerability through densely hatched lines and luminous chiaroscuro. This impression bears full, untrimmed margins and rich plate tone characteristic of early pulls. Its provenance traces from a private collection in Westmount, Quebec, to Waddington’s (Toronto) in 2019 and again in 2025, confirming a continuous and well-documented ownership history.

Printed in subtle gradations of rose, ochre, and gold, the work exemplifies Yoshida’s technical brilliance and sensitivity to human form. Each lifetime impression bears the artist’s pencil signature, title, and the red jizuri (self-printed) seal—attesting that the print was pulled under Yoshida’s direct supervision at his Tokyo workshop. The present sheet, noted for its luminous mica background and well-preserved color balance, descends from a Toronto private collection and was acquired at Waddington’s Editions Sale (October 2025). Comparable impressions have achieved strong results at Mainichi Auction (Tokyo) and Bonhams (London), underscoring its desirability among collectors of early modern Japanese printmaking.

Y57.value: This offset lithograph belongs to Takashi Murakami’s celebrated “And Then” series, characterized by immersive and hypnotic chromatic intensity. Dominated by a deep ultramarine ground, the composition is animated by subtle variations in color—particularly in the eyes and facial elements—giving each impression a distinctive visual rhythm despite its serial format. Murakami’s offset prints are produced through highly controlled, multi-stage processes that achieve exceptional sharpness, saturation, and surface complexity. For collectors, the work is especially appealing as a refined example of Murakami’s print practice, combining technical sophistication, visual richness, and the quiet uniqueness that distinguishes individual impressions within this iconic series.

Y58.value: LeRoy Neiman (American, 1921–2012) is known for his energetic, expressionistic style and vibrant portrayals of sports, entertainment, and leisure culture. “High Sea Sailings” showcases Neiman’s layered color approach and active mark-making, capturing both motion and atmosphere. This vibrant serigraph exemplifies LeRoy Neiman’s dynamic approach to movement, color, and spectacle, hallmarks of his celebrated late-career work. Known internationally for his depictions of major sporting and leisure events, Neiman captures the exhilaration of open-water sailing through energetic mark-making and saturated hues. Created in 1995, the print reflects the artist’s mature mastery of the serigraph medium, which allowed him to translate the spontaneity of his painting into richly layered color. For collectors, High Sea Sailings is especially appealing as a strong, recognizable example of Neiman’s iconic style, combining visual immediacy with the enduring popularity of his nautical and sports imagery in the secondary market.

Y59.value: This etching exemplifies Jean-François Millet’s radical elevation of rural labor to a subject of moral and artistic gravity, a vision that profoundly influenced later realists and modernists, including Van Gogh. The solitary figure—caught between effort and repose—embodies Millet’s belief in the quiet heroism of peasant life, rendered through an economy of line that gives the image unusual emotional force. Created during the height of the Barbizon movement, the work reflects Millet’s direct engagement with agricultural life around Barbizon rather than academic idealization. For collectors, Millet’s etchings are especially appealing for their rarity relative to his paintings and for offering a direct, intimate expression of the ideas that shaped nineteenth-century social realism.

Y60.value: This lithograph reflects Aristide Maillol’s classical approach to the female form, emphasizing harmony, weight, and sculptural calm. The seated nude, partially enveloped in drapery, is rendered with simplified contours and balanced proportions that echo Maillol’s work as a sculptor. Rejecting expressive excess, the composition conveys a timeless serenity rooted in classical tradition. The print exemplifies Maillol’s pursuit of idealized form and quiet monumentality in modern art. Presenting Sculptural serenity over anecdote or symbolism. Closely aligned with his work in stone and bronze, the composition demonstrates Maillol’s conviction that modern art could renew classical ideals through simplification and restraint. Unlike many printmakers, Maillol treated graphic works as extensions of his sculptural practice, giving his prints a distinctive sense of volume and permanence. Collectors value Maillol’s lithographs for their clarity of form and for providing access to the artist’s core aesthetic at a scale and intimacy unavailable in his monumental sculpture.

P61.value: Ginestet & Pouillon 670; very fine proof on vellum; numbered and signed in pencil by Picasso; mounted on cardboard; edition of 200; Bernheim-Jeune

Y61.value: Maternity reflects Picasso’s sustained engagement with themes of motherhood and tenderness during a pivotal period shaped by his relationship with Marie-Thérèse Walter. Executed in etching and aquatint with delicate color, the work demonstrates Picasso’s belief that printmaking could rival painting in emotional subtlety and formal invention. Images of maternity recur throughout his career, but works from this period are especially admired for their lyrical calm and classical balance. For collectors, the print offers a compelling combination of intimacy, technical sophistication, and a central theme within Picasso’s broader oeuvre. Maternity belongs to Picasso’s profound exploration of motherhood and familial intimacy during the late 1920s and early 1930s, a period shaped by his relationship with Marie-Thérèse Walter. Executed in etching and aquatint with subtle color, the work demonstrates Picasso’s mastery of printmaking as an expressive medium equal to painting. Images of maternity recur throughout Picasso’s career, but works from this period are particularly prized for their tenderness and classical calm. The composition bridges modern abstraction and ancient archetype, reinforcing Picasso’s ability to renew timeless themes through radical economy of form.

Y62.value: This etching forms part of Picasso’s celebrated Vollard Suite, widely regarded as one of the most important published print series of the twentieth century. Created during a period of intense personal and artistic experimentation, the composition explores intimacy and psychological tension through confident, economical line. The Vollard Suite marked Picasso’s full command of etching as a primary creative language, rather than a secondary medium. Collectors prize works from the suite for their art-historical importance, strong market demand, and for offering direct insight into Picasso’s evolving themes of desire, power, and human connection.
